# Buffered face saturation and the occupied-parity budget of a rigid stratum

This is a finite arithmetic and actual-fiber theorem. It does not prove OC
for an arbitrary original family. It sharpens the endpoint supplied by
whole-fiber rigidity and identifies exactly what happens when the buffered
face cover uses its entire occupied-parity budget.

The occupied-parity base center theorem used below is already proved in
`candidate 58dcf29bfb78a573`,
Sections 1--3. The actual graph argument refines
`candidate b5b06a687cb4f54a`:
its factor 2^n can be replaced by the occupied parity count of the complete
subfamily. The new buffered application uses only the independently audited
fixed-face equality theorem, not a hypothesis about continued deepest marks
under a body variation.

## 1. Finite lattice faces and their saturation

Let I be a finite nonempty subset of Z^n with

    I=conv(I) intersect Z^n.

All parities below mean congruence modulo 2Z^n. Write Q=conv(I), and let
F_p be the minimal face of Q containing p in its relative interior. Let
F_1,...,F_m be the inclusion-maximal members of {F_p:p in I}, and choose
p_i in I intersect relint(F_i). Write k=k(I) for the number of occupied
parities. Faces may be lower dimensional, and Q itself is an allowed face.

**Theorem 1.** One has m<=k. Moreover the following are equivalent:

1. m=k;
2. I consists of exactly k vertices of Q, one of each occupied parity.

In that case all the F_i are singleton vertices.

Proof. If p_i,p_j have the same parity, their midpoint is in I. Its minimal
face contains both F_i and F_j: a face containing an interior point of a
segment contains its endpoints, and a face containing p_i contains F_i.
That minimal face is contained in one of the chosen maximal faces.
Maximality forces F_i=F_j. Thus the m witnesses have distinct parities.

Now suppose m=k. For every z in I, its parity is that of a unique p_i.
The midpoint of z and p_i belongs to I. Its minimal face contains F_i
and z. Maximality of F_i therefore puts z in F_i. The midpoint belongs
to relint(F_i), because p_i does and z belongs to F_i. Its parity must
again be that of p_i: a relative-interior point of F_i with the parity
of p_j would give the preceding midpoint argument with F_i and F_j.
Repeatedly replace z by (z+p_i)/2. Every resulting point is an integer
point with the parity of p_i. Hence z-p_i is divisible by arbitrarily
large powers of two in Z^n, and z=p_i. Thus I={p_1,...,p_m}.

No p_i can be a nonvertex of Q. Otherwise F_i has a vertex v different
from p_i; this vertex is p_j for some j, and F_j={v} is properly contained
in F_i, contradicting the chosen maximality of F_j. This proves 1=>2.
Conversely, if all points of I are vertices of different parities, their
minimal faces are exactly those k singleton vertices. The rank-zero case
is included. QED.

The repeated-midpoint argument is important. Merely knowing that two
witnesses have distinct parities would not exclude other points of those
same parities on lower-dimensional faces.

## 2. Components of maximal faces retain all anchored relations

Join two maximal faces when their intersection is nonempty. Their
intersection is then a face of the lattice polytope Q and contains a
vertex in I. For each connected component of this finite graph let
J_c be the union of I intersect F_i over its faces. The J_c partition I:
a point belonging to two maximal faces connects those faces.

**Lemma 2.** Each J_c is lattice-complete, distinct J_c occupy disjoint
parity sets, and EVERY integer-anchored convex representation in I is
contained in one J_c. Consequently

    k(I)=sum_c k(J_c).                                      (1)

Proof. Suppose z=sum_l lambda_l z_l is in I, with all lambda_l>0 and
z_l in I. The face F_z contains every z_l by the defining face property.
Choose a maximal F_i containing F_z. Each z_l belongs to a maximal face,
which intersects F_i at z_l. Thus z and every z_l belong to the same
component. If z is an integer point of conv(J_c), completeness of I
puts it in I, and the argument puts it in J_c; this proves completeness.
For same-parity z,z' in I their integer midpoint is an anchored
representation, so they lie in one component. This proves (1). QED.

Conversely every maximal face is joined by anchored representations:
its chosen relative-interior lattice witness can be represented using
strictly positive coefficients on all its vertices, and any other point
of that face can be inserted with a sufficiently small positive weight.
Thus these are the full anchored-relation components; this construction
is NOT the generally inadequate midpoint-only component construction.

Let m_c count maximal faces in component c, and k_c=k(J_c). The convex
hull of J_c is a face subconfiguration rather than necessarily a face of
Q, but its minimal-face structure has the same maximal faces F_i in this
component. Indeed every original F_i remains a face of conv(J_c), and
every z in J_c has its original F_z as its minimal face there: intersect
with the original supporting equations, and use z in relint(F_z).
Theorem 1 applied to J_c now proves

    m_c<=k_c,
    m_c=k_c iff J_c is a singleton.                        (2)

For the last implication, Theorem 1 makes all maximal faces singleton;
connectedness then leaves one face. If r is the number of nonsingleton
components, summing gives the useful quantitative restriction

    m<=k(I)-r.                                             (3)

Thus with a deficit of one group from the parity budget, at most one
nontrivial anchored component can occur. Equation (3) does not bound
that component's number of bases or mass.

## 3. Occupied-parity centers of compatible translation graphs

Let J be a nonempty complete lattice base. If its affine span has smaller
rank, its inherited saturated affine lattice has exactly the same parity
relation on J: an ambient integer half-difference lies in that direction
space and hence in its saturated lattice. Thus the occupied-parity base
theorem uses precisely k(J) below. Suppose its positive
full-dimensional fibers in R^d, d>=1, are

    K_z=c_z+K,

with one fixed convex body K, and all actual integer-anchored Minkowski
inclusions hold. Compactness and support functions give

    c_z=sum_l lambda_l c_(z_l)
    whenever z=sum_l lambda_l z_l belongs to J.             (4)

Indeed inclusion of a nonzero translate of a bounded convex body into
itself is impossible. Therefore the convex hull G of graph points
(z,c_z) has exactly the singleton fiber {(z,c_z)} over every integer
base z in conv(J). This statement does not assert that c_z is one affine
function on the real base hull.

Give the graph points positive weights w_z, total W. Set k_J=k(J).
The occupied-parity base theorem supplies p in J with base halfspace
weight at least W/k_J. Equivalently p belongs to conv(A) for every
A subset J with w(A)>W-W/k_J: if p failed membership, strict separation
from the finite convex hull would give a closed base halfspace through
p missing A and carrying less than W/k_J.

For every such A, the graph hull over A has a point over p, and its
singleton integer-fiber property forces this point to be (p,c_p).
Thus (p,c_p) lies in EVERY large-weight graph hull. If an ambient closed
halfspace containing (p,c_p) had graph weight below W/k_J, its strictly
excluded finite graph subset would be one of these large sets, a
contradiction. Hence this single graph point has ambient graph depth
at least W/k_J. Closed boundary atoms have not been discarded.

Let g be the centroid of K, V=|K|, and Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d. With equal
weights V, the point (p,c_p+g) belongs to the actual family. Every ambient
halfspace containing it includes, on graph weight at least |J|V/k_J,
a translate of a continuous through-g cap. Ordinary Grunbaum, summed
on those original fibers, proves

    D_raw({(z,K_z):z in J}) >= Gamma_d |J|V/k_J.             (5)

Pure integer caps include each selected fiber wholly, so (5) also holds
for them. For n=0 the graph is one point, k_J=1, and this is precisely the
ordinary theorem. External constant fiber densities w_z/V give the same
auxiliary weighted statement Gamma_d W/k_J; the original application
uses the actual volumes.

This is a consequence of an ALREADY PROVED occupied-parity theorem,
not an unproved general replacement of a mixed Helly number by k(J).

## 4. Application to the actual buffered deepest stratum

Fix an actual compatible positive-d-volume family S on complete base P,
with original total mass M and original maximal raw depth Q_0. Fix a
sufficiently small positive buffer parameter in the audited energy-power
construction, and let I be its set of maximizing integer bases.

The fixed-body buffered theorem proves all the following premises:

* I is lattice-complete;
* at every maximal minimal face F_i there is exactly one deepest mark y_z
  over each integer z in F_i;
* all marked whole fibers K_z-y_z on that face coincide;
* the marks interpolate affinely within that face.

These statements hold for the normalized invariant version too, since
for the fixed body it differs only by a fixed norm and a positive scalar.
Every base in I lies in a maximal face, so its mark y_z is unique globally.
On an intersection of two faces the same actual marked fiber is present;
therefore equality propagates along the component graph of Section 2.
For each J_c there is one full body L_c such that

    K_z=y_z+L_c,                 z in J_c.                  (6)

All anchored relations within J_c satisfy (4), either from the face
premises and Lemma 2 or directly from actual compatibility and equal
centered bodies. Put M_c=sum_(z in J_c)|K_z| and M_I=sum_c M_c.

Apply (5) separately to each actual component. Its valid center is an
original point of S, and all other original fibers add nonnegative cap
mass. Thus Q_0, the ORIGINAL global maximum, satisfies

    Q_0 >= Gamma_d max_c M_c/k_c
        >= Gamma_d M_I/k(I).                              (7)

The second inequality is the weighted average bound using (1). This
combines numerical lower bounds on the SAME global maximum; it does
not average the separately selected component centers.

Equation (7) improves the 2^n denominator for a single rigid class and
pays the ENTIRE mass of the buffered deepest stratum. It still supplies
no payment for the original fibers outside I. In particular, if I=P
for any sufficiently small positive buffer, (7) proves the sharp occupied-
parity target for this original family. No such exhaustion is asserted.

If beta=Q_0/M is hypothetically below Gamma_d/k(P), (7) forces

    M_I/M <= beta k(I)/Gamma_d < k(I)/k(P),
    (M-M_I)/M >= 1-beta k(I)/Gamma_d.                       (8)

This is a quantitative surviving-mass condition, not a contradiction.
It does not require the additional attained-minimum proper-minor quotas.

## 5. What saturation removes, and what remains

If the fixed buffered witness count uses the full budget m=k(P), then

    m=k(I)=k(P),

and Theorem 1 says that I consists of parity-distinct vertices of conv(I).
Every contact set J_i in the exact buffered covering derivative is then
a singleton. The minimum over several marked source fibers disappears.
In particular there are NO nontrivial integer-anchored relations among
these deepest bases: a vertex cannot be a convex combination of the others.
Thus a proposed midpoint aggregation only among these witnesses has no
arithmetic relation on which to act. Any missing payment must retain
actual contacts or anchored relations involving nondeepest bases, or use
some other geometric information. This is a structural limitation, not
a counterexample to a contact-sensitive loss theorem.

The exact interval example
`candidate 75dd33535e246a34` has ORIGINAL,
unbuffered deepest base set I_0={1,2}, m=k(I_0)=k(P)=2, and all four
original fibers strictly below M/2. Endpoint common-cap cores fail for
every regular ordinary critical circuit at source 1. Its depth lies above
OC. This calibrates the arithmetic saturation and the endpoint-core
obstruction only. Its positive-buffer maximizing bases have not been
identified here and are NOT asserted to remain {1,2}.

If m<k(P), (3) quantifies some arithmetic slack but does not convert it
into a cap-loss ratio. In particular this note does not claim that a
projective source erosion is free at the other fibers, that the selected
weights have any prescribed lower bound, or that the first-order contact
minimum and all normalization costs can be omitted.


## 6. A regular selected row makes the corrected support strict

This strengthens the already saved regular-row/singleton-minimal-face
consequence in Section 13 of
`candidate 86dd5366456916a8`.
It concerns the PARTICULAR corrected resultant ell of a chosen group,
not only its source's minimal face.

Continue with the fixed energy-power buffered construction. At source
(p,y), write f_p=f(p,y), and let selected positive weights rho_j and actual
Q_epsilon-mass caps satisfy

    H_j={a_j.(z-p)+u_j.(x-y)>=-epsilon f_p},
    sum_j rho_j u_j=epsilon g,   sum_j rho_j=1,
    f(z,x)<=f_p+alpha.(z-p)+g.(x-y),
    ell=sum_j rho_j a_j-epsilon alpha.

Continuous normals are normalized in the fixed body norm; in particular
that norm does not depend on the integer tilt a_j. The previous theorem
gives ell.(r-p)<=0 for every other maximizing integer base r. Assume at
least ONE positively weighted cap H_j is C1 in the full actual hyperplane
parameters (a,u,c), with positive total mixed coarea.

**Proposition 6.** Then

    ell.(r-p)<0  for every r in I different from p.             (9)

Proof. Suppose equality holds, and choose any maximizing mark (r,Y). Its
quantile inequalities give, for every selected cap,

    d_j=a_j.(r-p)+u_j.(Y-y)-epsilon[f(r,Y)-f_p]<=0.

Their weighted sum equals epsilon times the nonnegative supergradient
deficit because ell.(r-p)=0. It is also nonpositive, so it is zero, the
deficit vanishes, and every d_j=0. Thus each SAME fixed physical cap H_j
is an attaining buffered cap at both (p,y) and (r,Y).

At the stated regular row, vary only its unrestricted integer tilt a,
holding u fixed. Differentiating its actual mass through a buffered
source (s,X) gives S (bar z-s), where S>0 is the mixed coarea and bar z
is the integer barycenter of its actual section. The buffer value at
that fixed source is independent of a. Since the cap attains the infimum
of all directional masses, this derivative is zero. Applying it at the
two sources forces bar z=p and bar z=r, contradiction. The same argument
works in the affine span of a lower-rank base. QED.

Thus the corrected supporting face intersects I only at p; since its
vertices belong to I, it is exactly the singleton {p}. In particular, if
a chosen corrected support face has positive dimension, NONE of its
positively weighted rows can have the stated full regularity. A proper
own section alone is insufficient for this regularity: supporting
facets of other fibers can carry nonzero one-sided coarea responses.

For polytopal positive-dimensional fibers, a failure of this regularity
at a cap having a proper own section requires at least one actual
supporting trace in another fiber with positive (d-1)-measure. Lower-
dimensional tangent traces do not produce the relevant jump. This is a
local geometric restriction, not an assertion of a new parity class or
of any required allocation weight at that supporting contact.
